newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Cook Islands deny Malaysian bidding for key assets.
newsitem.headline: Cook Islands deny Malaysian bidding for key assets.

text.p: The cash-strapped Cook Islands government on Thursday denied it had received an offer from a Malaysian tycoon to buy its prime assets, which are up for sale.

The Cook Islands Press this week reported that Malaysian billionaire Tajudin Ramli was behind a NZ$100 million (US$70.6 million) offer for nearly everything on the government's asset sale list, including Nikao International Airport.
Ramli is chairman of Malaysia's national carrier, Malaysian Airline System Bhd, of which he owns 32 percent.
Opposition party leader Norman George warned the sale of state assets to an Asian buyer would meet with vigorous resistance in the South Pacific Island nation.

"It's going to turn us into foreigners in our own country. It's like being occupied," he told Radio New Zealand International, adding that the sales would be opposed even if a European buyer were involved.

"The term 'foreign' just doesn't blend nicely with our people here and I can assure you that we won't allow it to happen. Even if the government goes ahead with it they will be asking for trouble, and they will get it."
But government spokesman Tap Pryor flatly denied an offer had been received from the Malaysian businessman. "We read about it in the Press and it was a complete surprise to us," Pryor told Reuters.
"We obviously would entertain bona fide expressions of interest through normal channels, but we have not received one from that person or any other Malaysian for the advertised assets."
The Cook Islands are bankrupt. The tiny island group, with a population of less than 20,000, has run up a public debt of US$120 million.

Assets up for grabs include the two national banks, the electricity, airport and port authorities, Telecom Cook Islands and the inventory of the government liquor store. But Pryor said their privatisation was not driven purely by a need for cash.

"That is a nice little by-product of it -- you bring in some funds and you pay off current debts -- but the larger policy is to shrink government, to get government out of business and to bring in investors and operators of professional calibre."
He said considerable interest had been expressed by companies in Australia, New Zealand, the United States and further afield, but declined to name them.
